Q: Unix script for masking sensitive data in the log files? A:

This might work for you (GNU sed):

sed '/^Phone\|^DOB\|^Pin/!b;h;s/\S*\s*//;s/[^-]/X/g;H;x;s/\(\S*\)\n\(\S*\)/\2/' file

Explanation:

  • /^Phone\|^DOB\|^Pin/!b only process lines beginning Phone, DOB or Pin (add more here)
  • h copy pattern space (PS) to hold space (HS) i.e. make a copy of the current line.
  • s/\S*\s*// delete the first first field and following white space.
  • s/[^-]/X/g replace all occurrences of -'s with X's in the remaining field.
  • H append a newline and then the PS to the HS.
  • x swap HS with PS
  • s/\(\S*\)\n\(\S*\)/\2/ replace the original second field with the amended one.

An alternative approach is:

sed -E ':a;s/^((phone|pin|dob) [X-]*)[^X-]/\1X/i;ta' file

Q: Is there a mechanism to loop x times in ES6 (ECMAScript 6) without mutable variables? A:

Since the introduction of iterator helpers in ECMAScript 2025, you can do:

Array(10).keys().forEach((_, i) => {
    console.log(i * 10);
});

This does not populate an array of the given length (as Array.from would do), and so the memory for it is constant, no matter what the provided length is for it. The forEach method here is not the Array method, but the Iterator method.

Note that if you just need a string repeated you can use String.prototype.repeat.

console.log("0".repeat(10))
// 0000000000

Q: how do you add a property to an existing type in TypeScript? A:

Intersection Type

In typescript, If you want to add members, you can use an intersection type:

type DateWithNewMember = T & { newMember: boolean }

Where T is the type you want to add member to.

Then use like this:

dates: DateWithNewMember<Date>[];

Union Type

You could use Union type:

class newDateClass {
   readonly fullYearUTC: number;
}

Then use like this:

date: Date | newDateClass

Q: Can't make a request to web API on local machine from handheld running Flutter A:

The localhost hostname is relative to the device making the request. While localhost:3000 on your desktop/laptop has the web server, making a request to localhost:3000 from your mobile device sends the request to your mobile device, which doesn't have a web server running. This is what causes the "Connection refused" error; your mobile device refused to connect to itself on port 3000.

The way around this is to:

  1. Use the IP address of your desktop/laptop running the web server, so https://192.x.x.x:3000 (replace 192.x.x.x with the IP address of your other computer running the web server).

  2. Set up your own DNS server within your local area network, and configure your mobile device to use your local DNS server for DNS lookups.

Back in the day, some mobile browsers refused to make requests to IP addresses, but that's been 15 years. The easiest thing to do is use the IP address of your computer running the web server.

Q: GCC specs file: how to get the installation path A:

After messing around with it for a while, I discovered that this actually is possible, using an undocumented GCC spec function called find-file (which has been supported since 2010). This function essentially does the same thing as gcc --print-file-name "some-filename", where it prints the path to a file with the given name within the library search paths. (Unlike --print-file-name, it returns NULL if the file is not found, instead of returning the original string).

The trick is to add a folder with a unique name somewhere inside the specific lib folders that are only used by this one version of GCC that you built. In my example, I added a folder inside /opt/gcc-spec-test/1-gcc-install/lib/gcc/x86_64-linux-gnu/14.3.0 named .custom-anchor-UNIQUE_SUFFIX. Now I can use %:find-file(.custom-anchor-UNIQUE_SUFFIX) to refer to the absolute path to that file.

Now let's say the path we actually want for the rpath is /opt/gcc-spec-test/1-gcc-install/lib64. Since .custom-anchor-UNIQUE_SUFFIX is a folder, we can also refer to this as /opt/gcc-spec-test/1-gcc-install/lib/gcc/x86_64-linux-gnu/14.3.0/.custom-anchor-UNIQUE_SUFFIX/../../../../../lib64. Now unfortunately, we can't just use %:find-file(.custom-anchor-UNIQUE_SUFFIX)/../../../../../lib64 inside a spec file, since the file(...) and what comes after it get split into two separate arguments. However we actually can do %:find-file(/opt/gcc-spec-test/1-gcc-install/lib/gcc/x86_64-linux-gnu/14.3.0/.custom-anchor-UNIQUE_SUFFIX/../../../../../lib64) with the additional paths inside the parentheses (this is somewhat surprising, but you can try it yourself with something like gcc --print-file x86_64-linux-gnu/..).

And that's it. Now you can put -rpath=%:find-file(.custom-anchor-UNIQUE_SUFFIX/../../../../../lib64) in your spec file.

If you want to have some additional safety and only do this if that unique folder actually exists, you can do something like %{%:if-exists(%:find-file(.custom-anchor-UNIQUE_SUFFIX)): -rpath=%:find-file(.custom-anchor-UNIQUE_SUFFIX/../../../../../lib64); :%eCould not find anchor folder} which raises an error "Could not find anchor folder" if for whatever reason the custom folder is not found.

A useful reference for learning about GCC spec files is Geoff Wozniak's blog posts:

  • Part 1: https://wozniak.ca/blog/2024/01/02/1/index.html
  • Part 2: https://wozniak.ca/blog/2024/01/09/1/
  • Part 3 (draft, seemingly removed): https://web.archive.org/web/20250801114034/https://wozniak.ca/blog/drafts/gcc-specs-3.html

Q: Does Java still have a strong future in the AI era? What should a fresher Java developer focus on for high-growth career opportunities? A:

Kotlin has had enough time to take that lead, it hasn't. Java (as a language) is pervasive because it is already the leading language in large code bases. Companies are not going to invest hundreds of millions of dollars into changing to a different language only to end up with the same product with more bugs in it. Where Java is, it will stay. And where Java is used, people will use Java for new appendages as well.
